page: Microsoft Azure D64s_v6 is a general purpose instance built on the x86_64 architecture and managed via Microsoft Hyper-V. It features a dedicated Intel Xeon 8573C processor running at up to 4.2 GHz across 32 physical cores and 64 vCPUs (2 threads per core). The processor includes 48 KB of L1d cache, 2 MB of L2 cache, and 260 MB of shared L3 cache, with hardware instruction support for AVX-512, AMX (tile and int8), and hardware cryptography (AES, VAES, SHA-NI). Memory capacity stands at 256.0 GB of RAM, sustaining a balanced 1:4 vCPU-to-memory ratio of 4.0 GB per vCPU. The instance does not include a GPU and has no local ephemeral storage, requiring remote storage solutions for persistent data.

Benchmark evaluations indicate broad strength across compute and memory subsystems. The instance scored 21795.0 on Geekbench multi-core and 73628.05 on PassMark CPU, placing in the top tiers. Read-only cached memory bandwidth peaked at 4665.0 GB/sec, while uncached large-block reads and writes reached 259.69 GB/sec and 110.72 GB/sec respectively. High-throughput operations perform well, evidenced by static web serving throughput of 97.36 GB/sec and 82.05 million Redis SET operations per second. PassMark database operations scored 32965.93, also placing in the top 10%.

Hardware-level vector and matrix instructions drive solid CPU-based machine learning performance, with 7B model prompt processing achieving 270.18 tokens/sec and text generation reaching 38.39 tokens/sec. Single-threaded benchmarks, such as stress-ng single-core (1950.38) and bzip3 decompression (13.06 GB/sec), sit in the middle 50% category. Large 70B model generation settles into the average band at 4.34 tokens/sec, illustrating the throughput limitations of CPU execution for larger generative models compared to dedicated accelerators.

Qualitatively, the D64s_v6 balances density and capability for large enterprise workloads requiring substantial CPU and memory scales without dedicated hardware accelerators. The absence of local disk implies that IOPS-heavy configurations will rely entirely on external network-attached volumes. This instance fits enterprise database hosting, large-scale Redis caching, concurrent web serving tiers, software compilation pipelines, and CPU-driven inference tasks.
